entry.title: Donald Trump Discusses Potential Jensen Huang Pardon and Congressional Testimony
entry.content:
Links: nypost.com

President Donald Trump stated in an exclusive interview that he is willing to pardon reinstated Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang if necessary, though he believes a pardon will not be required. Trump urged Huang to tell the truth during his upcoming testimonies before the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Banking Committee, adding that he does not believe Huang needs to invoke his Fifth Amendment rights.

Huang's recent reinstatement followed a brief departure amid intense congressional scrutiny over his ties to an alleged Chinese spy and multiple workplace affairs. Lawmakers have expressed skepticism and intend to question Huang regarding potential national security risks and export control violations, while Trump defended Nvidia's critical role in maintaining American artificial intelligence dominance.

entry.title: Ex-OpenAI Engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan Released on $1M Bond
entry.content:
Links: bloomberg.com

A federal judge has ordered former OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan released on a $1 million bond, concluding that prosecutors lacked sufficient evidence to keep him detained. Alfozan was previously jailed after being accused of installing a listening device in an executive conference room at the company.

His release conditions include a $500,000 cash component, surety from three acquaintances, travel restrictions confined to Northern California, and mandatory electronic monitoring via an ankle bracelet. The ruling follows an earlier October decision where a judge had denied bail over flight-risk concerns despite a bond offer from the Saudi consulate.

entry.title: Huawei Convicted in US of Stealing Trade Secrets and Bank Fraud
entry.content:
Links: apnews.com

A U.S. jury convicted Chinese technology giant Huawei of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud following a lengthy trial where prosecutors argued the company systematically misappropriated intellectual property from competitors and partners. However, jurors acquitted Huawei of the most serious charge of engaging in a criminal racketeering conspiracy, which lawyers for the company described as a major vindication that repudiated the government's central narrative.

The trial focused on allegations that Huawei stole technological secrets, operated in nations subject to U.S. sanctions such as Iran and North Korea, and made false statements to officials and banks. Defense attorneys argued the case relied on isolated instances of misconduct by employees rather than a coordinated corporate conspiracy, and announced plans to appeal the convictions while noting the company will maintain its global operations outside the United States.

entry.title: US Attorney General Blanche and FBI Director Patel Dodge Questions Regarding Jensen Huang Investigation

Huang was reinstated following his recent resignation amid allegations of improper relationships and concerns regarding the potential diversion of advanced semiconductor chips to China in violation of export laws. While Blanche defended Nvidia as a corporate citizen and downplayed active export investigations, both officials avoided specifics regarding ongoing inquiries or intelligence assessments concerning Huang and associated entities.

The settlement addresses complaints that the retailer failed to meet delivery promises, suppressed negative feedback, and made false claims about its cotton origins.

The agreement requires Shein to pay consumer redress and overhaul aspects of its operational and review practices to resolve the federal probe. Regulatory scrutiny of the company has intensified across multiple jurisdictions in recent months over consumer protection and environmental claims.

entry.title: Michael Harley: LLM Agents Serve Their Parent Companies Rather Than Users
entry.content:
Links: michaelharley.net | hacker news

Writer Michael Harley examines how frontier AI models prioritize corporate interests over user intent after encountering restrictions while attempting to purchase music from independent artists. When an AI agent built using Claude Code refused to help bypass a bot challenge on Bandcamp, Harley noted the contradiction that the same system readily downloaded audio files from YouTube without compensating creators.

Harley argues that corporate-controlled AI models enforce restrictions aligned with the commercial and legal priorities of their parent companies rather than the user's actual goals. This dynamic risks turning AI tools into heavily managed platforms driven by corporate policy or advertising, underscoring the need for local, open models that serve the user exclusively.

entry.title: Governor Hochul Signs Bill Restricting Vehicle Subscription Fees
entry.content:
Links: governor.ny.gov | hacker news

Governor Kathy Hochul signed a bill prohibiting motor vehicle manufacturers, dealers, and third-party providers from charging subscription fees for vehicle features that utilize pre-installed hardware without ongoing costs. The legislation specifically addresses recurring charges for functionality such as heated seats, enhanced navigation, and hands-free driving, which the state characterizes as exploitative practices.

Taking effect on February 27, 2027, the law (S.9348A/A.10411A) aims to establish clear rules against deceptive business models as automotive technology advances. The measure is part of a broader state effort to mitigate the cost of living by eliminating "junk fees" and ensuring consumers are not charged for features already included in the vehicle's purchase price.

entry.title: Google Maps Fails to Include West Bank Movement Restrictions
entry.content:
Links: wired.com

Google Maps lacks data on the hundreds of checkpoints and movement restrictions in the occupied West Bank, making it unreliable for Palestinian drivers. A former product manager spent over six years attempting to develop a prototype that highlighted administrative zones and warned users of permanent checkpoints. Although these features were briefly launched, Google retracted the update in late 2025 following complaints from Israeli media about navigation "glitches."

The rollback occurred amid Google's increasing involvement with Israel through the acquisition of Waze and the Project Nimbus contract. Despite the company's ability to map complex regions worldwide, it omitted the West Bank restrictions to avoid conflict with local interests. Palestinian drivers now rely on grassroots crowdsourcing, such as the Road Conditions Telegram channel, to navigate the region's hazardous travel infrastructure.

entry.title: Australia Reaches Agreement on Digital Duty of Care Legislation
entry.content:
Links: theconversation.com

The Australian government has secured an agreement with the Greens to pass its digital duty of care bill, which requires technology companies to address foreseeable online harms and introduces a private right of action for users. The updated legislation incorporates maximum fines of up to 5% of global revenue for non-compliance, alongside new dispute resolution pathways and expanded powers for the eSafety Commissioner.

This legal shift allows individuals and groups to initiate litigation against platforms for breaches of duty, moving regulatory enforcement beyond government agencies alone. While low-risk small businesses will be exempt and a 12-month transition period will apply, the bill lacks bipartisan support from the Coalition and introduces heightened legal exposure for major tech platforms operating in Australia.

entry.title: Oregon and Virginia Sue SpaceX Over Grok's "Spicy Mode"
entry.content:
Links: nytimes.com

The states of Oregon and Virginia have filed lawsuits against SpaceX, alleging that its Grok Imagine artificial intelligence tool violated consumer protection laws. The suits claim that Grok's "spicy mode" enabled the creation of more than 1.8 million sexualized images of women and at least 65 images of children. The legal actions argue that the company marketed the tool as safe while failing to implement standard safeguards against generating nonconsensual and explicit content.

These lawsuits are the first state-level actions against SpaceX regarding Grok's content generation. They follow a January 2026 bipartisan letter from 35 attorneys general demanding that xAI restrict the production of intimate and child sexual abuse material. The litigation highlights growing regulatory scrutiny over "nudification" technologies and the legal responsibilities of AI developers in preventing the generation of nonconsensual deepfakes.

While China is actively developing its own AI for military use, internal studies express concern that such technology may make its nuclear forces more vulnerable to rapid strikes. The research highlights a strategic shift where the increased speed of AI-integrated warfare could erode traditional stability and create a high-pressure environment for potential conflict.

entry.title: National Governors Association Proposes Federal and State Split for AI Regulation
entry.content:
Links: bloomberg.com | nga.org

The National Governors Association (NGA) has proposed a dual-layered framework for artificial intelligence governance, urging the federal government to oversee national and international risks associated with high-powered AI models. Under this plan, the federal government would conduct model reviews while individual states retain the authority to regulate AI use and protect consumers following deployment.

This bipartisan initiative, spearheaded by the Governors Council to Secure American AI Dominance, aims to provide a roadmap for the upcoming Congress. By separating model-level oversight from end-use regulation, the proposal seeks to ensure a unified national security stance on systemic risks while preserving the flexibility of state governments to adapt rules to local needs.
